title: Quiz 2 · High-yield pre-quiz
description: Two selected questions per Quiz 2 lecture entry. Prioritized from the formative, test banks and important physiology MCQs. Actual exam questions may differ.
selection_method: Manual selection of core mechanisms, recognisable clinical patterns and source-emphasized concepts; no prediction guarantee. Three clearly labelled lecture-based supplements fill source-bank gaps.

lectures.title: Normal Development of Heart & it’s Great Vessels
lectures.subject: Anatomy & Histology

questions.stem: When a baby is born and takes its first breath, the change in pulmonary pressure causes which embryonic vessel to constrict?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: B — Ductus arteriosus.
questions.selection_reason: Fetal circulation at birth and primitive heart-tube derivatives.

questions.stem: Which of the following cardiac structures represents the caudal end of the primitive heart tube?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: A — Sinus venosus.
questions.selection_reason: Fetal circulation at birth and primitive heart-tube derivatives.

lectures.title: Congenital anomalies of the heart & it’s great Vessels
lectures.subject: Anatomy & Histology

questions.stem: During normal atrial septation, the ostium secundum forms by resorption in which region?
questions.explanation: Perforations in the upper septum primum coalesce to form the ostium secundum. A secundum ASD is a separate abnormal persistence or deficiency that may involve excessive primum resorption or inadequate secundum development.
questions.selection_reason: Atrial septation and conotruncal defects.

questions.stem: A newborn has a single arterial trunk that overrides a ventricular septal defect and supplies both the systemic and pulmonary circulations. Which developmental failure explains this?
questions.explanation: Persistent truncus arteriosus results from failure of conotruncal separation into aorta and pulmonary trunk. A single trunk supplies both circulations and usually overlies a VSD.
questions.selection_reason: Atrial septation and conotruncal defects.

lectures.title: Anatomy of the nose and paranasal sinuses
lectures.subject: Anatomy & Histology

questions.stem: Which of the following paranasal sinuses opens into the nasal cavity through superior meatus?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: A — Posterior ethmoidal.
questions.selection_reason: Paranasal sinus drainage and the poorly draining maxillary sinus.

questions.stem: Which paranasal sinus is classically prone to poor drainage because its ostium lies high on its medial wall?
questions.explanation: The maxillary ostium is high relative to the sinus floor; the stem now tests drainage anatomy explicitly.
questions.selection_reason: Paranasal sinus drainage and the poorly draining maxillary sinus.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the main action of the transverse arytenoid muscle?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: D — Adduct the vocal cords.
questions.selection_reason: Vocal-cord adductors versus the sole abductor.

questions.stem: During thyroidectomy, a surgeon accidentally damages a nerve supplying a muscle that opens the vocal cords. Which muscle is affected?
questions.explanation: Source-bank key: Posterior cricoarytenoid. This is the supplied past-paper key; a detailed explanation has not yet been reviewed.
questions.selection_reason: Vocal-cord adductors versus the sole abductor.

lectures.title: Anatomy of the pleura and lungs
lectures.subject: Anatomy & Histology

questions.stem: Which pleural fluid color/appearance is most suggestive of a chylothorax?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: C — White (milky)
questions.selection_reason: Pleural-fluid appearance and the causes of a transudate.

questions.stem: Which of the following will yield a transudate fluid?
questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: Pleural-fluid appearance and the causes of a transudate.

questions.stem: What impressions can we find on the mediastinal surface of the left lung?

options.A: The groove for the descending aorta.
options.B: The groove for the azygos vein
options.D: The groove of the superior vena cava.

questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: A — The groove for the descending aorta.
questions.selection_reason: Right-versus-left mediastinal lung impressions.

questions.stem: Which chamber of the heart mainly forms the cardiac impression on the medial surface of the right lung?
questions.explanation: Source-bank key: Right atrium. This is the supplied past-paper key; a detailed explanation has not yet been reviewed.
questions.selection_reason: Right-versus-left mediastinal lung impressions.

questions.stem: The commonest congenital anomaly of trachea and esophagus is:
questions.explanation: Source-bank key: Esophageal atresia and tracheo-esophageal fistula. This is the supplied past-paper key; a detailed explanation has not yet been reviewed.
questions.selection_reason: Tracheoesophageal abnormalities and embryonic tissue origins.

questions.stem: The epithelium of the respiratory tract comes from which of the following?
questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: Tracheoesophageal abnormalities and embryonic tissue origins.

questions.stem: A child born at 26 weeks survives with intensive care but develops respiratory distress due to insufficient surfactant. This condition is due to improper function of which one of the following cells?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: A — Type (II) pneumocytes.
questions.selection_reason: Type II pneumocytes and structural differences along the airways.

questions.stem: Which of the following portions of the respiratory tract lack smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: C — Alveoli.
questions.selection_reason: Type II pneumocytes and structural differences along the airways.

questions.stem: Which of the following rib (s) articulates with the 4th thoracic vertebra?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: C — 4th & 5th ribs.
questions.selection_reason: Rib articulations and the intercostal neurovascular bundle.

questions.stem: An instrument damages the main neurovascular bundle in a rib's costal groove. What is its order from superior to inferior?
questions.explanation: The main intercostal bundle lies in the costal groove in VAN order from above downward.
questions.selection_reason: Rib articulations and the intercostal neurovascular bundle.

questions.stem: The maximum decrease in ventricular pressure occurs during:
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: B — Isovolumetric relaxation phase.
questions.selection_reason: Isovolumetric phases, valve position and ventricular pressure.

questions.stem: During the isovolumetric contraction phase of the cardiac cycle, which of the following best describes the change in ventricular pressure?

options.A: Ventricular pressure remains unchanged while ventricular volume increases rapidly.
options.B: Ventricular pressure increases rapidly while ventricular volume remains constant.
options.C: Ventricular pressure decreases rapidly while ventricular volume remains constant.
options.D: Ventricular pressure increases gradually while ventricular volume decreases.

questions.explanation: Ventricular pressure rises while all valves are closed; ventricular volume remains constant during isovolumetric contraction.
questions.selection_reason: Isovolumetric phases, valve position and ventricular pressure.

questions.stem: Which part of the ECG corresponds to the plateau phase (Phase 2) of the ventricular action potential?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: C — ST segment
questions.selection_reason: ECG segments and heart-rate calculation.

questions.stem: An ECG shows a regular rhythm with 4 large squares between consecutive R waves. Assuming standard ECG paper speed, what is the approximate heart rate?
questions.explanation: For a regular rhythm at standard paper speed, heart rate is approximately 300 divided by the number of large squares between R waves: 300/4 = 75 beats/min.
questions.selection_reason: ECG segments and heart-rate calculation.

questions.stem: What is the earliest classic ECG change in hyperkalemia?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: B — Tall, peaked T waves
questions.selection_reason: Hyperkalemia and recognition of atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: Which feature is characteristic of atrial fibrillation?

options.A: Regular rhythm with identical P waves before every QRS
options.B: Absence of organized P waves with an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm
options.D: Prolonged PR interval with progressively dropped QRS complexes

questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation causes loss of organized P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm.
questions.selection_reason: Hyperkalemia and recognition of atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has had poorly controlled hypertension for several years. Recent investigations suggest impaired endothelial function in his systemic arteries. Which endothelial change would most likely contribute to increased vascular tone in this patient?

options.D: Increased inhibition of smooth muscle contraction

questions.explanation: Reduced nitric oxide availability impairs endothelium-dependent vasodilation and contributes to increased vascular resistance.
questions.selection_reason: Endothelial nitric oxide and antithrombotic function.

questions.stem: A healthy blood vessel is exposed to normal blood flow without any vascular injury. Which endothelial response is most important for preventing unnecessary thrombus formation?

options.A: Release of mediators that reduce platelet adhesion.
options.B: Release of mediators that supress fibrinolysis.
options.C: Expression of surface proteins that enhance thrombin generation.
options.D: Secretion of factors that promote coagulation.

questions.explanation: Healthy endothelium releases antiplatelet mediators such as nitric oxide and prostacyclin, limiting platelet adhesion and aggregation.
questions.selection_reason: Endothelial nitric oxide and antithrombotic function.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after sustaining a penetrating injury to the right side of his chest. On examination, breath sounds are markedly reduced on the right side, and a chest X-ray shows a right-sided pneumothorax. Which pressure change most likely caused the collapse of the affected lung?

options.B: Loss of the normal negative intrapleural pressure

questions.explanation: The supplied question bank marks B: Loss of the normal negative intrapleural pressure
questions.selection_reason: Pressure changes in inspiration and pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A healthy person takes a deep inspiration. Which combination of changes occurs?

options.A: Diaphragm contracts, thoracic volume increases, alveolar pressure decreases
options.B: External intercostals relax, thoracic volume increases, alveolar pressure increases
options.C: Diaphragm relaxes, thoracic volume decreases, alveolar pressure increases
options.D: Diaphragm contracts, thoracic volume decreases, alveolar pressure increases

questions.explanation: The supplied question bank marks A: Diaphragm contracts, thoracic volume increases, alveolar pressure decreases
questions.selection_reason: Pressure changes in inspiration and pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with progressive shortness of breath is diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis. Pulmonary function tests were performed. Which combination of changes would most likely be present?

options.A: Increased compliance and increased lung volumes
options.B: Normal compliance with markedly increased airway resistance
options.C: Decreased compliance and increased work of breathing
options.D: Increased compliance and reduced elastic recoil

questions.explanation: The supplied question bank marks C: Decreased compliance and increased work of breathing
questions.selection_reason: Fibrosis, compliance and surfactant function.

questions.stem: What is the primary function of pulmonary surfactant?

options.A: Reduce alveolar surface tension and prevent alveolar collapse

questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: A — Reduce alveolar surface tension and prevent alveolar collapse
questions.selection_reason: Fibrosis, compliance and surfactant function.

lectures.title: Gas diffusion and plumonary blood flow
lectures.subject: Physiology

questions.stem: According to Fick’s law of diffusion, gas diffusion across the respiratory membrane increases when:
questions.explanation: The supplied question bank marks A: The partial-pressure gradient increases
questions.selection_reason: Fick’s law and matching perfusion to ventilation.

questions.stem: As part of regulating pulmonary blood flow, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) due to local alveolar collapse will result in:
questions.explanation: The supplied question bank marks C: Decrease perfusion to non-ventilated segment.
questions.selection_reason: Fick’s law and matching perfusion to ventilation.

questions.stem: The oxygen-haemoglobin (O2-Hb) dissociation curve demonstrate that:

options.A: Hb binds irreversibly to oxygen when O_{2} partial pressure is low.
options.B: Hb releases more O_{2} when the O_{2} partial pressure is lower than 40 mmHg.
options.C: Hb releases more O_{2} when the O_{2} partial pressure is higher than 90 mmHg.
options.D: Hb binds irreversibly to oxygen when O_{2} partial pressure is high.

questions.explanation: The supplied question bank marks B: Hb releases more O_{2} when the O_{2} partial pressure is lower than 40 mmHg.
questions.selection_reason: Oxygen unloading and the rightward shift during exercise.

questions.stem: During vigorous exercise, skeletal muscle temperature and CO_{2} production increase. What happens to the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve?

options.A: Shifts to the right, increasing oxygen affinity
options.B: Shifts to the left, facilitating oxygen delivery
options.C: Shifts to the right, facilitating oxygen delivery
options.D: Shifts to the left, increasing oxygen affinity

questions.explanation: The supplied question bank marks C: Shifts to the right, facilitating oxygen delivery
questions.selection_reason: Oxygen unloading and the rightward shift during exercise.

lectures.title: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood
lectures.subject: Physiology

questions.stem: The largest proportion of CO_{2} in blood is transported in the form of:
questions.explanation: The supplied question bank marks B: Bicarbonate ions
questions.selection_reason: Bicarbonate transport and the Haldane effect.

questions.stem: As blood reaches the pulmonary capillaries, oxygen binds to hemoglobin. How does this facilitate CO_{2} unloading?

options.B: Oxygen binding causes chloride to remain permanently inside RBCs
options.C: Oxygen binding promotes release of CO_{2} and H from hemoglobin
options.D: Oxygen binding increases hemoglobin’s ability to bind CO_{2}

questions.explanation: The supplied question bank marks C: Oxygen binding promotes release of CO_{2} and H from hemoglobin
questions.selection_reason: Bicarbonate transport and the Haldane effect.

questions.stem: Which region of the brainstem contains the major respiratory centers responsible for generating the basic respiratory rhythm?
questions.explanation: The supplied question bank marks C: Medulla
questions.selection_reason: Medullary rhythm generation and lung stretch reflexes.

questions.stem: Hering-Breuer reflex from:

options.D: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata

questions.explanation: Source-bank key: Lung stretch receptor. This is the supplied past-paper key; a detailed explanation has not yet been reviewed.
questions.selection_reason: Medullary rhythm generation and lung stretch reflexes.

questions.stem: A person voluntarily holds their breath. After a period of time, the increasing urge to breathe becomes difficult to suppress. Which change contributes most strongly to this response?

options.A: Increased arterial O_{2} stimulating pulmonary stretch receptors
options.B: Increased arterial CO_{2} and H concentration stimulating chemoreceptors
options.C: Increase plasma H⁺ which stimulates Hering-Breuer reflex.
options.D: Decreased arterial O_{2} which stimulate central chemoreceptors.

questions.explanation: The supplied question bank marks B: Increased arterial CO_{2} and H concentration stimulating chemoreceptors
questions.selection_reason: Carbon dioxide drive and the peripheral oxygen threshold.

questions.stem: Peripheral chemoreceptors are most sensitive when partial pressure of oxygen falls below?
questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: Carbon dioxide drive and the peripheral oxygen threshold.

questions.stem: A patient has normal arterial PaO2 but tissue hypoxia, elevated venous oxygen and impaired cellular oxygen utilization. Which listed mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Histotoxic hypoxia is failure of cellular oxygen utilization, such as mitochondrial enzyme inhibition. The original failure-to-improve-with-oxygen clue alone could also suggest a shunt and was insufficient.
questions.selection_reason: Histotoxic hypoxia and shunt-related hypoxemia.

questions.stem: A patient remains hypoxaemic despite 100% inspired oxygen because venous blood bypasses ventilated alveoli. Which mechanism explains this?
questions.explanation: Shunted blood does not contact ventilated alveoli, limiting the response to oxygen. The original nonspecific stem was ambiguous.
questions.selection_reason: Histotoxic hypoxia and shunt-related hypoxemia.

lectures.title: Metabolic functions of the lung and Pulmonary Surfactant
lectures.subject: Biochemistry

questions.stem: A premature newborn develops respiratory distress due to deficient pulmonary surfactant. Which listed phospholipid is its main surface-active constituent?
questions.explanation: Source-bank key: Dipalmitoyl phosphatidyl chloride. This is the supplied past-paper key; a detailed explanation has not yet been reviewed.
questions.selection_reason: DPPC and the metabolic role of pulmonary ACE.

questions.stem: How does the pulmonary vascular endothelium help inactivate circulating bradykinin?
questions.explanation: ACE on pulmonary endothelial surfaces degrades bradykinin. The original key describing histamine release did not answer the intended metabolic-clearance question.
questions.selection_reason: DPPC and the metabolic role of pulmonary ACE.

lectures.title: Acid-base homeostasis and the role of the respiratory system
lectures.subject: Biochemistry

questions.stem: A diabetic patient with glucose 600 mg/dL and confirmed ketoacidosis has pH 7.27, PaCO2 25 mmHg and bicarbonate 11 mmol/L. Which respiratory response compensates for the metabolic acidosis?
questions.explanation: Metabolic acidosis stimulates hyperventilation, lowering PaCO2. These values are mutually consistent and PaCO2 is near the expected compensatory range (1.5 × 11 + 8, approximately 24.5 ± 2 mmHg).
questions.selection_reason: ABG interpretation and respiratory compensation.

questions.stem: a 24 year old women came to ER with SOB , the result of ABG shows ph=7.27, pco2= 60, po2= 65, HCO3=26, base excess +1 . what is the diagnosis?

options.A: Acute respiratory acidosis with only a small bicarbonate rise

questions.explanation: Elevated PaCO2 with acidemia indicates acute respiratory acidosis. Bicarbonate can rise slightly from immediate buffering before substantial renal compensation develops.
questions.selection_reason: ABG interpretation and respiratory compensation.

questions.stem: Which is included in the pathogenesis of primary hypertension?
questions.explanation: Impaired natriuresis can sustain volume expansion and contribute to essential hypertension; renal or adrenal diseases are secondary causes.
questions.selection_reason: Sodium handling and pressure-overload hypertrophy.

questions.stem: Which listed condition produces chronic left ventricular pressure overload and concentric hypertrophy?
questions.explanation: Systemic hypertension raises left ventricular afterload. The incomplete preload option was replaced with an explicit volume-overload distractor.
questions.selection_reason: Sodium handling and pressure-overload hypertrophy.

questions.stem: A patient over 50 has new temporal headache, scalp tenderness and visual symptoms. Which vascular disease should be suspected?
questions.explanation: New temporal headache in an older adult, especially with jaw claudication or visual symptoms, suggests giant cell arteritis.
questions.selection_reason: Clinical recognition of large-vessel vasculitis.

questions.stem: Vasculitis of the aorta and its branches?
questions.explanation: The keyed answer follows from the characteristic vessel layer, lesion morphology, or disease association described in the stem.
questions.selection_reason: Clinical recognition of large-vessel vasculitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is considered to be a major revised Jones criteria?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: B — Polyarthritis
questions.selection_reason: Jones criteria and the consequence of aortic stenosis.

questions.stem: Long-standing severe aortic stenosis produces pressure overload of which chamber, leading to which listed change?
questions.explanation: Aortic stenosis raises left ventricular afterload and causes concentric left ventricular hypertrophy. The valve lesion is explicitly supplied rather than inferred from a small photograph.
questions.selection_reason: Jones criteria and the consequence of aortic stenosis.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of a prosthetic aortic valve presents with fever and a new heart murmur. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Which of the following is the most likely type of infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: D — Acute infective endocarditis
questions.selection_reason: Acute infection and systemic embolic complications.

questions.stem: 36 year old woman , blood cultures are positive for gram positive bacteria. Urine analysis show hematuria. An echocardiogram shows a 1.5 cm vegetation on the mitral valve. Which of the following conditions is this patient most likely to develop?
questions.explanation: Left-sided infective endocarditis can send septic emboli into systemic arteries and cause cerebral infected aneurysms. Hematuria may reflect immune-complex glomerulonephritis.
questions.selection_reason: Acute infection and systemic embolic complications.

questions.stem: An immunocompromised patient has violaceous vascular nodules on the feet with spindle cells and slit-like vascular spaces. Which virus is associated with this lesion?
questions.explanation: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which can form violaceous nodules on the feet. Nodules alone are nonspecific.
questions.selection_reason: HHV-8 vascular tumors and cardiac metastases.

questions.stem: Which of the following are common primary sites of cancer that can metastasize to the heart?
questions.explanation: Lung and breast cancers commonly metastasize to the heart, particularly the pericardium.
questions.selection_reason: HHV-8 vascular tumors and cardiac metastases.

questions.stem: A small glottic cancer is detected early because it changes the voice. What additional feature favors its prognosis?
questions.explanation: Early hoarseness and limited true-cord lymphatics support earlier diagnosis and less early nodal spread.
questions.selection_reason: Glottic prognosis and EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

questions.stem: A nasopharyngeal biopsy shows large undifferentiated epithelial cells in a dense lymphoid background and EBER positivity. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The lymphoepithelioma pattern of NPC has malignant epithelial cells with reactive lymphocytes and a strong EBV association.
questions.selection_reason: Glottic prognosis and EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

questions.stem: Primary atelectasis is defined as:

options.A: Reduction in size of a previously expanded lung due to compression
options.B: Reduction in lung size due to contraction
options.C: Reduction in size of a lung due to obstruction
options.D: Incomplete expansion of a previously unexpanded lung

questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: D — Incomplete expansion of a previously unexpanded lung
questions.selection_reason: Primary versus obstructive/resorption atelectasis.

questions.stem: Bronchial obstruction by mucus in bronchiectasis can cause which type of atelectasis?
questions.explanation: Mucus obstruction associated with bronchiectasis can lead to resorption atelectasis.
questions.selection_reason: Primary versus obstructive/resorption atelectasis.

questions.stem: Serum IgE levels are elevated in:
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: B — Extrinsic bronchial asthma
questions.selection_reason: Atopic asthma and airway remodeling.

questions.stem: Which structural change contributes to persistent airflow obstruction in chronic asthma?

options.A: Destruction of alveolar septa with loss of elastic recoil

questions.explanation: Subepithelial fibrosis and smooth-muscle hypertrophy are components of airway remodelling that can make obstruction less reversible.
questions.selection_reason: Atopic asthma and airway remodeling.

questions.stem: A patient with confirmed alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency has cirrhosis and emphysema. Which emphysema pattern is classically associated with this inherited disorder?
questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and the Reid index.

questions.stem: What does the Reid index measure?

options.A: Submucosal mucus-gland thickness divided by bronchial wall thickness from epithelium to cartilage
options.B: Cartilage thickness divided by total bronchial wall thickness
options.C: Mucosal thickness divided by total bronchial wall thickness
options.D: Muscle thickness divided by total bronchial wall thickness

questions.explanation: The Reid index compares the thickness of bronchial submucosal mucus glands with bronchial wall thickness.
questions.selection_reason: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and the Reid index.

questions.stem: 50-year old female patient came with Dry cough , Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with Non-caseating granuloma . He had:
questions.explanation: Source-bank key: SARCOIDOSIS. This is the supplied past-paper key; a detailed explanation has not yet been reviewed.
questions.selection_reason: Sarcoidosis and restrictive spirometry.

questions.stem: (Case) A patient came in with interstitial fibrosis. What may be the result of the pulmonary function test?
questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: Sarcoidosis and restrictive spirometry.

questions.stem: Lines of Zahn help distinguish a thrombus formed in flowing blood from a postmortem clot. Where may they occur?
questions.explanation: Alternating platelet/fibrin and red-cell layers form in flowing blood; both arterial and venous thrombi may show them.
questions.selection_reason: Antemortem thrombi and pulmonary vascular remodeling.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old patient came to the ER with pulmonary hypertension. What is the most common change that occurs in his arteries?
questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: Antemortem thrombi and pulmonary vascular remodeling.

questions.stem: Which clinical setting increases the risk of nosocomial pneumonia?

options.A: Brief admission for minor elective surgery
options.D: Prolonged antibiotic therapy and mechanical ventilation

questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: D — Prolonged antibiotic therapy and mechanical ventilation
questions.selection_reason: Hospital-acquired infection and aspiration lung abscess.

questions.stem: An alcohol-dependent patient with impaired consciousness develops foul-smelling sputum and a lung abscess in the posterior upper-lobe segment after aspiration while supine. Which listed mechanism best explains it?

options.A: Aspiration of bacteria-containing oropharyngeal material during impaired consciousness

questions.explanation: Aspiration of contaminated oropharyngeal material can cause a lung abscess, often in dependent segments. Gastric aspiration may initially cause chemical pneumonitis, with secondary infection possible.
questions.selection_reason: Hospital-acquired infection and aspiration lung abscess.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman who has never smoked presents with persistent cough and weight loss. CT scan reveals a peripheral lung mass. Histology shows malignant glandular cells containing mucin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: D — Adenocarcinoma
questions.selection_reason: Adenocarcinoma versus squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: A smoker has a cavitating lung tumour with keratin pearls. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges support squamous cell carcinoma, often associated with smoking and central cavitation.
questions.selection_reason: Adenocarcinoma versus squamous cell carcinoma.

lectures.title: Drugs used in the treatment of bronchial asthma
lectures.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct drug–clinical use combination?

options.A: Albuterol — used as monotherapy in persistent asthma
options.B: Theophylline — has strong anti-inflammatory effects in chronic asthma
options.C: Salmeterol— used alone for acute asthma attacks
options.D: Cromolyn — inhibits mast cell degranulation and is used as prophylactic control therapy

questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: D — Cromolyn — inhibits mast cell degranulation and is used as prophylactic control therapy
questions.selection_reason: Controller mechanisms and inhaled corticosteroid adverse effects.

questions.stem: Which of the following drugs are used in asthma and cause hoarseness of voice and candidiasis ?
questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: Controller mechanisms and inhaled corticosteroid adverse effects.

questions.stem: In case of Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection, the suggested treatment will be?
questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: Atypical organisms and beta-lactamase inhibition.

questions.stem: Which drug is given to overcome the resistance of beta-lactamase-producing bacteria?
questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: Atypical organisms and beta-lactamase inhibition.

lectures.title: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 1
lectures.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem: Which listed long-acting muscarinic antagonist is used as maintenance bronchodilator therapy in COPD?
questions.explanation: Tiotropium provides long-acting muscarinic blockade; no COPD medication is free of adverse effects.
questions.selection_reason: LAMA therapy and mucolytic effects.

questions.stem: Which effect describes a mucolytic drug?

options.A: Stimulates the mucociliary activity of the respiratory epithelium
options.D: Reduces the viscosity of respiratory secretions

questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: LAMA therapy and mucolytic effects.

lectures.title: Drug therapy of cough and COPD 2
lectures.subject: Pharmacology

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with COPD has persistent exertional dyspnoea despite appropriate inhaled therapy. Which non-pharmacological intervention is most likely to improve his exercise capacity and quality of life?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: B — Pulmonary rehabilitation
questions.selection_reason: Pulmonary rehabilitation and adding a second long-acting bronchodilator.

questions.stem: A 69 years-old man has COPD with moderate airway obstruction. Despite using salmeterol two times daily, he reports continued symptoms of shortness of breath with mild exertion. Which agent is an appropriate addition to his current therapy?
questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: Pulmonary rehabilitation and adding a second long-acting bronchodilator.

questions.stem: A diabetic patient receiving antihypertensive treatment has recurrent hypoglycemia. Which listed drug class can mask adrenergic warning signs such as tachycardia?
questions.explanation: Beta blockers can mask adrenergic hypoglycemia symptoms. Diabetes or peripheral arterial disease alone is not a blanket absolute contraindication to the entire class.
questions.selection_reason: Beta-blocker adverse effects and clonidine withdrawal.

questions.stem: Abruptly stopping which centrally acting antihypertensive can cause marked rebound sympathetic activation and severe hypertension?
questions.explanation: Clonidine withdrawal can cause rebound hypertension. The drug is an antihypertensive; the original antianginal description was misleading.
questions.selection_reason: Beta-blocker adverse effects and clonidine withdrawal.

questions.stem: Which drug should be avoided in a hypertensive patient with bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis affecting a solitary functioning kidney?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibition can markedly reduce GFR in bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis of the artery to a solitary functioning kidney. Unilateral stenosis is not an automatic contraindication.
questions.selection_reason: RAAS-blocker contraindications and hydralazine compensation.

questions.stem: Which combination counters hydralazine-induced reflex tachycardia and sodium/fluid retention?
questions.explanation: Hydralazine can provoke reflex tachycardia and sodium retention; a beta blocker and diuretic counter these effects. This is the conventional hydralazine combination, not a complete modern heart failure regimen.
questions.selection_reason: RAAS-blocker contraindications and hydralazine compensation.

questions.stem: Which of the following drug–indication combinations is correct?

options.A: Verapamil — WPW with pre-excited atrial fibrillation

questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: D — IV magnesium — torsades de pointes
questions.selection_reason: Torsades treatment and antiarrhythmic mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which drug acts on Na+ and K+ channels to control arrhythmia?
questions.explanation: Answer preserved from the supplied past paper; consult the source page and current lecture when reviewing.
questions.selection_reason: Torsades treatment and antiarrhythmic mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which anti-TB drug–adverse effect pair is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: D — Isoniazid — peripheral neuropathy
questions.selection_reason: Isoniazid toxicity and the initial four-drug regimen.

questions.stem: An adult has confirmed drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis. In the standard six-month regimen, which combination is used during the initial two-month phase?
questions.explanation: The standard six-month regimen begins with two months of HRZE, followed by four months of isoniazid and rifampicin. Other recommended regimens exist for eligible patients; the stem specifically asks about the six-month regimen.
questions.selection_reason: Isoniazid toxicity and the initial four-drug regimen.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old farmer presents with a six-day history of cough, dyspnea, and fever. Stool examination reveals no parasitic eggs. Further investigations demonstrate eosinophilia and leukocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: B — Loeffler’s syndrome
questions.selection_reason: Loeffler syndrome versus acute schistosomiasis.

He was present with fever, cough wheeze myalgia headache and urticaria.stool analysis revealed 2-3 eggs of schistosoma mansoni. What is the stage?

lectures.title: Cystic parasitic diseases of the lung
lectures.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem: Hydatid disease through:

options.A: Direct skin penetration by filariform larvae
options.B: Eating raw vegetables contaminated by Echinococcus eggs
options.C: Drinking water containing only hookworm filariform larvae

questions.explanation: Hydatid disease follows ingestion of Echinococcus eggs from canid-faecal contamination of hands, food or water. It does not follow hookworm larvae or mosquito bites.
questions.selection_reason: Hydatid transmission and cyst rupture.

questions.stem: A farmer with dog exposure has a pulmonary cyst that ruptures, and imaging shows floating detached membranes. Which listed parasite causes this hydatid lesion?
questions.explanation: Detached cyst membranes support pulmonary echinococcosis; a homogeneous opacity alone did not establish hydatid disease.
questions.selection_reason: Hydatid transmission and cyst rupture.

questions.stem: What is the first-line treatment for streptococcal pharyngitis?
questions.explanation: Source-bank key: Penicillin. This is the supplied past-paper key; a detailed explanation has not yet been reviewed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a route of administration for the BCG vaccine?
questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: A — Intradermal
questions.selection_reason: BCG administration and bird-associated pneumonia.

questions.stem: A patient presents with fever and features of lower respiratory tract infection. He gives the history of keeping birds and parrots. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation: Bird exposure with pneumonia suggests Chlamydia psittaci. The corrupted merged alternative was separated.
questions.selection_reason: BCG administration and bird-associated pneumonia.

questions.stem: Which cell is primarily responsible for killing virus-infected respiratory epithelial cells through recognition of antigen presented on MHC class I molecules?

options.B: CD8+ cytotoxic T cell ( correct answer)

questions.explanation: Supplied formative answer: B — CD8+ cytotoxic T cell ( correct answer)
questions.selection_reason: CD8/MHC I antiviral immunity and IL-5/eosinophils.

questions.stem: Which Th2 cytokine promotes eosinophil production and activation?
questions.explanation: IL-5 promotes eosinophil differentiation, survival and activation. Chemokines such as eotaxin also regulate eosinophil recruitment into tissues.
questions.selection_reason: CD8/MHC I antiviral immunity and IL-5/eosinophils.
